prompt: Why do some people in Singapore stay with glasses and never try contact lenses?
answer_text:
In Singapore, some people stick with glasses for their entire lives and never even try contact lenses — even when they can afford them. 😄 It's usually not because they can't wear contacts. It's because glasses are comfortable, convenient, and simply good enough for them.

Here are some common reasons.

1. Glasses are much easier to manage
 

Glasses

Put them on and go

No touching your eyes

Easy to remove when tired

 

Contact lenses

Need clean hands

Require insertion and removal

Need proper cleaning or daily replacement

For someone who has worn glasses since primary school, contact lenses might feel like introducing an unnecessary chore into their routine.

2. Singapore's hot and humid weather

Singapore's climate can influence the decision, although it affects people differently.

Sweat: Glasses can slide down the nose during outdoor activities.

Air-conditioning: Spending hours in offices, classrooms and shopping malls can contribute to dry eyes, making contact lenses uncomfortable for some people.

Outdoor activities: Contacts can be convenient for sports, but dust, wind and sweat can also make wearing them less comfortable.

So the weather doesn't automatically make one option better. It depends on the person's eyes and lifestyle.

3. Some people are afraid of touching their eyes

This is a bigger factor than you might expect.

Some people feel uncomfortable with the idea of putting a lens directly onto their eyeball. They may worry about:

Accidentally scratching their eye.

Being unable to remove the lens.

Getting an eye infection.

Having something stuck in their eye.

Even though properly fitted contact lenses are generally safe when used correctly, someone who feels anxious about eye contact may never see a reason to overcome that fear.

4. Glasses are part of their identity and style
 
 
11
 

For some Singaporeans, glasses aren't just a medical device. They're a fashion accessory.

Glasses can make someone look:

More professional or mature.

More intellectual or studious.

More fashionable, depending on the frames.

More recognisable, because people are used to seeing them that way.

Some people actually feel that their face looks strange without glasses because they've worn them for so long.

5. They don't see enough benefit to justify the hassle

This is probably one of the biggest reasons.

Contact lenses offer advantages, especially for sports, dancing, outdoor activities and people who dislike frames obstructing their appearance. But if someone spends most of their time studying, working in an office, commuting on the MRT and relaxing at home, glasses may already meet all their needs.

Why spend extra money on contact lenses and take time to learn how to use them if glasses work perfectly well?

6. Cost and maintenance matter

Contact lenses can involve recurring expenses for lenses, solution and eye examinations, depending on the type used. Daily disposable lenses can be especially costly with everyday use.

Glasses also cost money, of course, but a well-maintained pair can last a long time if the prescription remains suitable and the frames stay in good condition.

7. Some simply have sensitive or dry eyes

Not everyone tolerates contact lenses equally well. People with dry eyes, allergies or certain eye conditions may find contacts uncomfortable or may need professional advice before using them.

They might have tried contacts once, found them irritating, and decided glasses were the better choice.

What about Singaporeans who have never tried contacts at all?

I'd roughly group them into four types:

Type

	

Typical reason




The practical person

	

"Glasses work. Why change?"




The cautious person

	

"I don't want to touch my eyeballs."




The comfort-first person

	

"I prefer not having anything on my eyes."




The glasses enthusiast

	

"My glasses suit my face."

Of course, these are informal categories, not measured statistics about Singaporeans.

My take: The interesting thing is that people who have never tried contact lenses often don't feel they're missing out. People who wear contacts regularly may love the freedom of having no frames, while lifelong glasses wearers may see contact lenses as extra work for very little benefit.

And there's one more interesting distinction: someone who has never tried contact lenses may have a very different reason from someone who tried them and stopped. The first might be afraid or uninterested; the second may already know that glasses suit them better.

It isn't necessarily a Singapore-only trend, but the local climate and lifestyle can make the drawbacks of contact lenses more noticeable.

The 6 most common reasons

1. Heat, humidity and sweat

Singapore's heat can make commuting and walking outdoors uncomfortable. Sweat, sunscreen and facial oils can also get around the eyes or onto lenses, making people more inclined to wear glasses.

 

2. Air-conditioning and dry eyes

Air-conditioned offices, shopping malls and buses can have relatively dry airflow. Contact lenses may worsen dryness, grittiness, irritation or that feeling of having something in your eye, particularly after hours of wear.

 

3. Long workdays and screen time

When people spend most of the day working on computers or looking at phones, they tend to blink less completely. This can destabilise the tear film and make contact lenses feel increasingly uncomfortable by evening.

 

4. Glasses are easier to maintain

Glasses can be put on in seconds. Contact lenses require clean hands, proper insertion and removal, and sometimes cleaning and storage. Daily disposable lenses remove the cleaning step, but they still require handling and replacement.

 

5. Cost adds up

Regular contact lens purchases, lens solutions and eye examinations can cost more over time than using one pair of glasses for everyday wear, although glasses also need replacement and prescription updates.

 

6. Glasses have become a style choice

Glasses are now a fashion accessory for many people. If they are comfortable, suit someone's face and work well for their routine, there may be little reason to tolerate contact lenses every day.

Is Singapore's climate really the main reason?

The stronger explanation is often dry eyes and contact lens intolerance, rather than humidity alone.

prompt: How do people in Singapore choose between LASIK, SMILE, ICL and contact lenses?
answer_text:
In Singapore, people usually choose between LASIK, SMILE, ICL and contact lenses by weighing four things: their prescription, corneal suitability, tolerance for eye dryness, and whether they want a permanent procedure or a reversible option.

There isn't one universally best choice. Someone with moderate short-sightedness and healthy corneas may have several options, while someone with very high myopia or a thin cornea may need a different approach.

1. The four options at a glance
 
LASIK

Laser reshaping of the cornea

A surgeon creates a thin corneal flap and reshapes the tissue underneath with a laser.

Often appeals to: People who want rapid visual recovery and are suitable for laser correction.

Trade-offs: Temporary dry eyes, possible glare or halos, and flap-related risks.

Key consideration: Corneal thickness, shape and overall eye health.

 
SMILE

Minimally invasive corneal laser surgery

A laser creates a small piece of tissue inside the cornea, which the surgeon removes through a small incision.

Often appeals to: People who want laser correction without a LASIK-style flap.

Trade-offs: Dry eye can still occur; early vision recovery may be less predictable or slower than LASIK for some people.

Key consideration: The type and range of prescription that the particular SMILE system is approved to treat.

 
ICL

An implant inside the eye

A lens is placed inside the eye, behind the iris and in front of the natural lens. The cornea is not reshaped.

Often appeals to: People with high myopia, or those whose corneas are unsuitable for laser surgery.

Trade-offs: Higher upfront cost, intraocular surgery risks and ongoing monitoring.

Key consideration: Adequate space inside the eye, eye pressure, endothelial cell count and lens suitability.

 
Contact lenses

Non-surgical and removable

Soft lenses or, where appropriate, rigid lenses correct vision without permanently changing the eye's structure.

Often appeals to: People who want flexibility, are not ready for surgery, or prefer to avoid surgical risks.

Trade-offs: Recurring costs, daily care or replacement, dryness and the risk of eye infection.

Key consideration: Comfort, hygiene, wear time and regular professional fitting.

2. How people typically decide

A useful way to think about the choice is to start with the problem each option solves.

If your main priority is…

	

Options worth discussing




Fast visual recovery

	

LASIK; SMILE is also an option




Avoiding a corneal flap

	

SMILE or ICL




Very high short-sightedness

	

ICL, depending on prescription and eye measurements




Reducing dependence on daily contact lenses

	

LASIK, SMILE or ICL if suitable




Avoiding surgery entirely

	

Contact lenses or glasses




Keeping your correction removable

	

Contact lenses; ICL is surgically removable but is not equivalent to a contact lens




Concern about dry eyes

	

Assess the underlying dryness first; contacts and all surgical options can cause problems

These are starting points, not rules. For example, SMILE may produce less early postoperative dryness than LASIK in some patients, but it is not a guaranteed solution for someone with chronic dry eye. ICL avoids corneal tissue removal, but it involves surgery inside the eye. 
National University Hospital

3. Cost in Singapore: upfront versus long-term

The financial decision can be quite different depending on whether you plan to wear contacts for another two years or another twenty.

Contact lenses

Recurring cost
Monthly or daily lenses, solutions where applicable, eye examinations and replacement supplies. You can spread the cost over time and stop whenever you choose.

LASIK and SMILE

Upfront cost
Typically a one-off surgical expense, plus assessment, medication and follow-up. The exact price depends on the provider, technology and prescription.

ICL

Higher surgical commitment
Custom implant lenses and intraocular surgery can make this a substantial upfront expense. Ask whether the quoted price includes both eyes, assessments and follow-up.

As a concrete Singapore reference point, the Singapore National Eye Centre lists ICL surgery at S$6,386–S$7,664 per eye, inclusive of 9% GST, for its stated fee categories as of 24 August 2026. This is an institutional fee, not a universal market price. 
Singapore National Eye Centre

For a fair comparison, ask clinics for an all-in quote and compare the same items: suitability assessment, surgery for both eyes, medication, follow-up visits and any enhancement policy. Also consider the cost of glasses you may still need later.

4. What about age, dry eyes and long-term vision?

Three factors can change the decision substantially.

Age and reading vision: Surgery can correct distance vision, but it does not stop presbyopia, the age-related loss of near focusing that commonly becomes noticeable in your 40s. You may still need reading glasses later.

Dry eyes: Singapore's air-conditioned offices, long screen hours and existing contact lens discomfort may make dry eye an important consideration. Have the tear film assessed before choosing a procedure; treating existing dryness first may be necessary.

Eye pressure, the health of the natural lens and retina.

For ICL, measurements to establish whether there is adequate space for the implant.

The findings determine which procedures are medically suitable and which are not.

In Singapore, when a teenager gets their first pair of contact lenses, parents and students usually need to balance eye health, safety, convenience, appearance, cost and the teenager’s readiness to manage the lenses independently.

It’s not just a question of which lenses to buy. For many families, it’s also about whether the teenager is ready to take responsibility for their eyes, and whether contact lenses are suitable for their school, CCA (co-curricular activities), sports and social life.

1. The main considerations for parents and teenagers
 
1. Eye health and professional fitting

Parents’ priority: safety and suitability.

Is the teenager’s prescription suitable for contact lenses?

Are their eyes healthy enough, including the tear film and cornea?

Do they have dry eyes, allergies or frequent eye irritation?

Can an optometrist teach them how to insert, remove and care for the lenses?

A professional contact lens fitting and follow-up are important, even if the teenager already wears glasses.

 
2. Hygiene and responsibility

Parents’ priority: can my child use them safely without constant reminders?

Teenagers need to wash and dry their hands before handling lenses, follow the prescribed wearing schedule, and never sleep or swim in lenses unless specifically advised by their eye-care professional.

Parents may also consider whether their child can remove a lens calmly if it becomes uncomfortable, recognise warning signs and ask for help when needed.

 
3. School, CCA and everyday convenience

Students’ priority: will contact lenses make daily life easier?

Common motivations include:

Playing sports without glasses slipping or fogging up.

Feeling more comfortable during PE lessons and outdoor activities.

Avoiding glasses interfering with dance, performances or other CCAs.

Having more freedom with hairstyles, photographs and personal style.

Families should also consider long school days, air-conditioned classrooms, outdoor exposure and whether the teenager can manage lens care between school and activities.

 
4. Lens type and comfort

The key question: which option fits the teenager’s eyes and routine?

Daily disposable lenses: a fresh pair each day, with no lens-storage case or routine cleaning required.

Reusable lenses: may cost less over time, but require the prescribed cleaning, disinfection and replacement schedule.

Clear versus coloured lenses: cosmetic preferences should never override fit, oxygen transmission, hygiene or eye health.

Daily disposables can be a convenient starting option for some teenagers, but the best choice depends on the fitting and professional advice.

 
5. Cost and value for money

Parents’ priority: what will this cost over a full year?

Families should look beyond the price of the first box. Consider:

The cost of regular lens supplies.

Professional fitting and follow-up visits.

Cleaning solutions and cases, if needed.

Replacement lenses, backup glasses and unexpected appointments.

A low introductory price is less useful if the lenses are uncomfortable or the ongoing costs are difficult to sustain.

 
6. Confidence, appearance and peer influence

Students’ priority: how will I look and feel?

Some teenagers want to see their face without glasses, feel more confident in photos or fit their preferred style. Others may feel curious because their friends wear contact lenses.

Parents can acknowledge these motivations while helping their teenager understand that contact lenses are a medical device, not simply a fashion accessory.

Use a registered eye-care professional. Contact lenses should be prescribed and dispensed through an appropriately registered optometrist or contact lens practitioner.

This is one of the biggest considerations, especially for people who already experience dry eyes from air-conditioning, prolonged screen use or contact lens wear.

2. They're concerned about permanent side effects

Most appropriately selected patients achieve good vision after laser surgery, but the outcomes aren't guaranteed to be perfect.

Glare, halos or starbursts around lights, particularly at night.

Difficulty driving at night, especially during the recovery period.

Persistent dry eyes or fluctuating vision.

Residual short-sightedness or astigmatism, sometimes requiring glasses, contact lenses or further treatment.

Rare but serious complications involving the cornea.

The important distinction is that contact lens problems are often manageable by changing the lenses or stopping wear, whereas some surgical complications can be difficult to reverse.

3. They may not be suitable candidates for surgery

Reasons include:

Thin corneas or an irregular corneal shape.

A prescription that is too high or unsuitable for the procedure.

Eyesight that is still changing.

Significant dry eye or other eye conditions.

Medical conditions or medications that may affect healing.

Swimming pools are treated with chlorine, but they are not sterile. Lakes, seawater and hot tubs can also contain microorganisms.

 

2. Lenses can trap germs against your eye

Contact lenses may interfere with the eye’s natural defences, allowing microbes to attach to the cornea and cause infection.

 

3. Goggles help, but do not eliminate the risk

Even well-fitting swimming goggles can leak. They reduce water exposure but do not make swimming in contact lenses risk-free.

The guidance from Singapore healthcare institutions is clear: do not swim, shower or sleep while wearing contact lenses.

If you must wear contacts

Ask your eye-care professional about your individual situation. A well-fitting pair of goggles over lenses may reduce exposure, but it cannot eliminate the infection risk. Daily disposable lenses do not make swimming safe.

What if you accidentally swim with contacts in?

Remove your lenses as soon as you can, using clean, dry hands.

If you wear reusable lenses, clean and disinfect them according to the manufacturer's instructions before wearing them again. If the lenses were submerged, discarding them is the more cautious option; discard daily disposables after use.

Never rinse or store lenses in tap water, bottled water or homemade saline.

Choose artificial tears specifically labelled as compatible with your contact lenses.

Reduce airflow and dryness

Avoid sitting directly in front of air-conditioning vents, fans or car air-conditioning outlets. Consider a clean humidifier if your indoor environment is particularly dry.

 

Give your eyes a break from contact lenses

Wear glasses when your eyes feel dry, gritty or tired. Follow your prescribed wearing schedule and replace disposable lenses on time. Never sleep or shower in lenses unless specifically advised for an approved lens-wearing regimen.

Lens fit and replacement schedule: whether the lenses fit properly and are being worn for an appropriate duration.
